'''Marvin D. Girardeau''' (3 October 1930 – 13 January 2015)<ref>{{cite news |url=https://uaatwork.arizona.edu/lqp/memoriam-marvin-d-girardeau |title=In Memoriam: Marvin D. Girardeau |date=22 January 2015 |author=University Relations - Communications |website=uaatwork.arizona.edu |publisher=Arizona University}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Marvin D. Girardeau |date=2 February 2015 |first=Adolfo |last=del Campo|journal=Physics Today |doi=10.1063/PT.5.6134 }}</ref> was a [[quantum]] [[physicist]], and a [[faculty (academic staff)|faculty]] member in the [[Institute for Theoretical Science]]  at the [[University of Oregon]], where he was hired as a professor in 1963 and worked until his retirement in 2000, after which he became a research professor at the [[University of Arizona]]. He was a mathematical physicist with an unusual nonlinear career, which culminated in a remarkable impact in the ultracold atom physics community.<ref>{{cite news |last1=del Campo |first1=Adolfo |title=Marvin D. Girardeau |journal=Physics Today |issue=DOI:10.1063/PT.5.6134 |date=2 Feb 2015|doi=10.1063/PT.5.6134 }}</ref> One of Girardeau's achievements was to predict the existence of the [[Tonks–Girardeau gas]] in 1960.   A Tonks–Girardeau gas was created in 2004, and its measured properties strikingly confirmed Girardeau's original predictions.

His research interests included the [[Dynamics (mechanics)|dynamics]] of [[ultracold]] [[atom]]ic [[vapour]] confined in tight [[Louis-Victor de Broglie|de Broglie]] [[waveguide]]s; and the behaviour of identical particles including [[fermion]]s, [[boson]]s, and [[anyon]]s.

Girardeau was a fellow of the [[American Physical Society]], and winner of the 1984 [[Humboldt Prize]]. His 1984-86 tenure at the [[Max Planck Institut für Strahlenchemie]], Mühlheim/Ruhr, Germany, followed. In 2013, Marvin was nominated for a prestigious Senior [[BEC Award]] by the European Community.
